newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian finance minister takes aim at IMF, Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Indian finance minister takes aim at IMF, Moody's.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram has dismissed criticism from the International Monetary Fund and U.S. credit rating agency Moody's, saying the IMF offers only "textbook" advice and Moody's was wrong.
Chidambaram was asked in an interview at the weekend to comment on an IMF report that said India could face a debt crisis unless it made deeper cuts in the fiscal deficit.
"That's out of a textbook. Running a government cannot be according to a textbook," he said.

The report by IMF economists, released last week, said that unless red ink was brought under stricter control, debt and interest payments could spiral upwards, leading to wider current account deficits and deteriorating debt indicators.
"An eventual external crisis would become unavoidable," the IMF said.
Chidambaram said: "I don't visualise that scenario."

"I visualise a scenario where we will make a fiscal correction as rapidly as possible, control inflation and maintain price stability, at the same time stimulate growth as well as appropriate large amounts of money for social sector programmes."
Asked if he was saying the IMF was not attuned to realities in India, the finance minister said: "IMF's dharma (belief) is to read out of textbooks."

The IMF helped India out of an economic crisis in the early 1990s but has been the object of some criticism, especially by the communist and right-wing Hindu parties, for allegedly dictating tough reform policies to New Delhi.
The IMF argues that without adjustment policies, strained economies will reach a breaking point.
Chidambaram was also asked to comment on a report last week by Moody's that stirred criticism by some Indian politicians.

The credit rating agency said India's unstable political environment, directionless economic policies and a deterioration in its macroeconomic balances had led Moody's to take an unfavourable outlook on the nation's sovereign rating.
"I think Moody's rating's wrong. I mean whoever gave them the inputs must have given it to them at least four months ago," Chidambaram said.

"It is quite evident that Moody's did not even take into account the budget," he said, referring to the tax and spending blueprint for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) which he presented to parliament last month and drew widespread praise.
Moody's, which upgraded India's rating from Ba2 to Baa3 in December, 1994, recently assessed potential pressure on the rating over an 18- to 24-month horizon.
